assessmentSummary.identity: Proposed base identity: a bilateral standing broad jump projected diagonally with approximately 90 degrees of body rotation, bilateral landing on a rotated target, and a deliberate two-second stick.
currentCardFindings: The legacy card names horizontal projection and rotation but never specifies turn angle, takeoff and landing laterality, direction, or hold.
Kicking-athlete transfer language is contextual rather than part of stable movement identity.
No difficulty, anatomy, load, fatigue, constraints, or distance and angle dosage are present.

population: can_absorb combined horizontal and rotational momentum

proposedDosage.progressWhen: both directions reach the target angle and distance with a quiet two-foot landing and no hand touch or extra step

coachCues: Bring the hips over the landing feet
Land on the rotated target and freeze
athleteInstructions: Jump forward and across from two feet
Land on two feet and hold
commonFaults: feet too far ahead of hips

readiness: mastered broad jump and bilateral quarter turn separately

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as a distinct combined horizontal-projection and rotation card only after fixing the base angle and bilateral contact sequence. Keep sport transfer in contextual profiles, not stable identity.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Rotational Broad Jump to Stick uses hip extension, trunk rotation, horizontal projection to improve a key kicking-athlete problem: Combines horizontal force, hip rotation, and a controlled finish, giving kickers a power drill that still respects landing mechanics.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Rotational jump identity must specify takeoff and landing laterality, turn angle and direction, projection vector, contact sequence, external height, rebound intent, and required stabilization.

Rotational Broad Jump to Stick must not combine bilateral jump turns, unilateral rotational bounds, multi-contact sequences, broad jumps, or repeated reactive turns under one generic rotational label.
A jump-to-stick combines ballistic propulsion with a deliberate landing and stabilization phase; repeated reactive hopping is a different task.

Rotational Broad Jump to Stick belongs to rotational jump or bound power with landing control, with direction, laterality, projection, contact sequence, and rebound intent encoded as controlled dimensions.
Propulsion and force absorption are coordinated across the foot and ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and trunk.

The card should assign task-specific roles to plantar flexors, intrinsic foot muscles, quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteals, hip stabilizers, obliques, and trunk stabilizers without treating lumbar rotation as the primary driver.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Plyometric demand changes with projection speed, direction, external height, body mass, and time available to produce and absorb force.

Observable quality includes the prescribed takeoff, whole-body turn led by foot-hip-trunk coordination, visual orientation before contact, intended flight path, quiet landing, knee tracking, stable pelvis and trunk, and ownership of the finish.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Plyometric intensity changes with speed, height, distance, body mass, laterality, external load, and movement complexity.

Exercise difficulty must score technical and physical demand directly, including spatial coordination, impact, supervision, work capacity, and consequence of error; exercise cards must not use skill-library levels.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Landing contacts, jump height or distance, turn angle, laterality, contact sequence, and external load govern mechanical exposure; power repetitions require adequate rest.

Rotational Broad Jump to Stick needs contact count per side and direction, output intent, impact and eccentric stress, spatial and technical-fatigue criteria, and recovery guidance rather than conditioning-style work time.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Effective jump-landing interventions depend on appropriate materials, coaching knowledge, usable space, and task-specific progression.

The delivery profile should require a level non-slip surface, clear flight and landing zones in every turn direction, adequate ceiling height, athlete spacing, coach sightline, and readiness for rotational orientation and landing.
Bilateral landing and stabilization should precede unilateral, larger-angle, farther, multi-contact, or reactive jumping.
Prescribe low-repetition sets, contacts per direction, turn angle, projection target, hold time, rest, and progression criteria; stop before fatigue alters orientation or landing.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Specific prescriptive feedback can improve landing mechanics, while excessive cue volume can interfere with learning.
Use a small cue set: load through the prescribed stance, turn the body as one coordinated unit, find the landing before contact, land quietly, and hold without a touch-down, shuffle, or rebound.
Loud contact, poor stabilization, loss of alignment, or inability to coordinate ankle, knee, and hip indicate excessive jump intensity or volume.
Stop for pain, giving way, dizziness, disorientation, repeated valgus or trunk collapse, forced lumbar twisting, missed turn angle, uncontrolled foot contact, extra steps, or loss of output.

evidence.sourceTitle: Evidence-Based Best-Practice Guidelines for Preventing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries in Young Female Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
evidence.sourcePublisher: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
claims: Landing stabilization and lower-body strength are recurring components of effective neuromuscular injury-prevention programs.

Rotational Broad Jump to Stick belongs after linear and lateral landing foundations and before fatigued multidirectional work; use low volume and sufficient recovery to preserve spatial and landing quality.

evidence.sourceTitle: The Use of Augmented Information for Reducing Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk During Jump Landings: A Systematic Review
claims: Athletes benefit from feedback tied to visible movement actions rather than abstract risk language.
Athlete support should show start and finish orientations, turn direction and angle, foot contact sequence, landing target and hold time, one primary cue, and the stop signal.

evidence.sourceTitle: Training interventions to reduce the risk of injury to the lower extremity joints during landing movements in adult athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims: Coach education and practical implementation affect whether jump-landing interventions are delivered effectively.

Coach support should provide front, side, and finish-angle observation, pass-fail criteria, contact counting, left-right comparison, regressions, progressions, and rules for reducing angle, distance, laterality, or contact count.
Beginners should establish bilateral landing and stabilization before progressing to unilateral, higher, farther, or reactive tasks.

Accessibility can be improved with start and finish floor arrows, visual targets, demonstrated orientations, reduced turn angle or distance, assistance, longer reset time, and reduced sensory demand without assigning an exercise skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Basics of Strength and Conditioning Manual
claims: Different turn angles, projection directions, laterality, landing stance, repeated contacts, obstacles, and external load have different intensity and programming implications.

Turn direction, small angle adjustments, and submaximal targets are usually variants; a different takeoff or landing laterality, projection vector, contact sequence, rebound intent, or testing purpose may require a distinct definition.
